The Homeland Security Act of 2002 also required DHS to consolidate existing federal government emergency response plans into a single, coordinated national response plan. In December 2004, DHS issued the National Response Plan (NRP), intended to be an all-discipline, all-hazards plan establishing a single, comprehensive framework for the management of domestic incidents where federal involvement is necessary. It is to
operate within the framework of NIMS. A crucial aspect of being able to successfully provide such coverage is the ability to obtain what the industry refers to as credible “vulnerability assessments” or risk assessments. To be useful, a risk assessment must be able to estimate both the likely “frequency” and “severity” of catastrophic events— two key characteristics that insurance companies need to assess the probability and financial significance of a loss. In addition, based on credible information, insurers must be able to estimate both their “probable maximum loss (PML),” an estimate of the maximum dollar value that can be lost under realistic conditions, and their “maximum foreseeable loss (MFL),” an estimate of the maximum dollar loss under a worst-case scenario. Risk assessments can be used to provide a basis for making loss projections for catastrophes such as hurricanes or earthquakes, although the projections may not be accurate. Insurance companies use these estimates to determine the amount of coverage and the price at which to offer coverage within a geographic area. Potential losses are acceptable if the probability that they may occur is understood and companies can set prices that fully reflect the consequences of a specific risk. When projections fail to anticipate an event, such as an earthquake, or underestimate the severity of an event, such as Hurricane Katrina, insurance companies may become insolvent, as happened in the aftermath of Hurricane Andrew, or may choose to reduce the amount of coverage offered in a given area, as happened for wind losses in Florida and for earthquakes in California.

Text_Content: What would another Hurricane Katrina bring in 2020? Is government at all levels ready for such an event? Or is the worst yet to come? (Kettl 2006). In the following sections, we argue that successful emergency preparedness, response, and recovery in the future are largely functions of the degree to which government leaders possess strategic management capacity. Such management is an ongoing process integrating planning that is issue focused, externally oriented, and opportunity seeking (Koteen 1997). We do not sound the alarm that is so common among post-9/11 and Katrina commentators, but rather offer a strategic framework to enhance our understanding of the importance of management and leadership before and during a Katrina-like event occurring in the year 2020. We cannot point to the characteristics of what an “ideal” response and recovery for any given situation or locale might look like in this short essay—if indeed such characteristics exist and could be identified—but we do offer perspectives on the critical managerial components of an emergency management strategy. Our observations are grounded in the notion that a “disaster occurs when the demands of the system are greater than the capabilities of the community to meet them” (Simpson 2008). Put another way, the impact of a disaster “agent” (such as a hurricane) alone does not determine whether an actual disaster occurred; it is also a question of whether the community has the requisite strategic capacity to effectively mitigate, address, and cope with the incident.

Text_Content: The emergency management field was a patchwork of relationships and requirements, and as broad as the type of risks that society faced. In addition to dealing with natural and technological disasters, public health threats, environmental issues resulting in economic loss, cyberterrorism, and even astronomical issues (e.g., the possibility of asteroid and meteor strikes) were all on the plate of the field. It was a challenge, even in an all-hazards environment, to find common ground for discussions about particular types of disasters, as well as to accommodate the wide variety of professional interests from civil engineering to health and human services to psychological counseling. Guidance and “best practices” emanated from both governmental and nongovernmental organizations, but rarely did one consistent set exist for a given area (Waugh 2007).

Text_Content: The use of strategic issues management, which addresses the primary strategic concerns of an organization or organizational system, is important in emergency management because of the occurrence of unexpected and surprise events. Koteen (1997) argues that the criteria for identifying strategic issues include assessing (1) the current or potential impact on organizational performance, (2) the perceived urgency in significant consequences, and (3) the impact or interdependency with other issues. For more than three decades, emergency management has been described in terms of a comprehensive, systems-based approach to activities comprising four management phases: mitigation, planning and preparedness, response, and recovery. However, most of the academic and popular literature has focused on one phase—emergency response— even as Hurricane Katrina exposed weaknesses in mitigation and recovery. Effective strategic management of disasters necessarily must focus on all issues and phases.

Drabek and McEntire note that “disasters, by their very disruptive and dynamic nature, create such significant demands on the affected community that well-executed, multiorganizational responses become not only necessary, but essential... Text_Content: Our understanding of how to lead such an all-encompassing, multiorganizational process in emergency management is emerging, but implementing such principles on the ground is still a work in progress (Kettl 2007). Although it may be extremely challenging to address hardware and software problems that create obstacles to interoperability in communications and to design a consistent and unifying solution, it is far more difficult to effectively address the timing, frequency, content, and scope of interorganizational and interpersonal collaboration. One recent study of U.S. counties demonstrated that only when emergency managers found themselves in situations in which the problems facing their organization were increasingly severe did they reach out to collaborate with other entities and agencies (McGuire and Silvia 2010). It was found that the extent and level of external management is a function not only of the severity of the problem faced by the county, but also the level of capacity possessed by the manager and his or her agency. Furthermore, leadership actions that mobilize external support for the emergency management network and facilitate interaction within the network were found to positively relate to network effectiveness (McGuire and Silvia 2009). Central to the perceived effectiveness of a network is its established legitimacy in the eyes of its stakeholders and a demonstrated commitment by local officials to make disaster preparedness its highest priority (McEntire and Myers 2004).

Text_Content: As Moynihan (2005) shows, responses to man-made disasters can take place, paradoxically, through collaboration governed by command and control procedures. His case study of the outbreak of Exotic Newcastle Disease in the state of California describes the administrative capacity of a task force assigned with limiting and eliminating the disease. The task force operated much like a lateral, side-by-side collaborative arrangement, but it did so within the context of a top-down incident command system. The emergency response network was coordinated hierarchically, suggesting the existence of a “hierarchical network” (Moynihan 2008) or working “from the top down so that the system works from the bottom up” (Kettl 2006, 283). Such an external orientation is one of the pillars of strategic emergency management.

Text_Content: Emergency management is a complex mix of individuals, organizations, and actions, some of which will not be necessary in many types of disasters and emergencies and others that will be singularly and perhaps unexpectedly important, with rules and expectations that are most times ambiguous, and which tends to be highly inter-disciplinary in nature. As a result, emergency managers and those who study the emerging field within public administration need to understand and appreciate a variety of disciplines. If viewed from one discipline or viewpoint, it is highly likely that important information, data, and insights will be missed, inhibiting our ability to completely understand individual catastrophes such as Katrina. For instance, it is important to understand not only the development and operation of bureaucratic organizations, but also interactions between organizations and networks within the organizations, communications, collective behavior, and individual social and psychological behavior in extreme environments (from the perspective of responders, and citizens and survivors alike).

Text_Content: Learning to manage actions supporting disaster response and recovery operations consistently and effectively requires strategic, not reactive, thinking. From some perspectives, developing the requisite capacity to manage disaster operations can appear to be equivalent to the fate of Sisyphus. There needs to be developed a common understanding of what adequate planning and preparedness looks like in a variety of situations, along with an always imperfect yet effective response and recovery. But how is this to be done, short of offering only speculative guidelines, standards, and measures? (Henstra 2010). What does competence look like? What are we expecting to see? What are the assumptions of government and expectations of the public? The answers to these questions can be derived only through strategic activity.

Text_Content: We are encouraged by the strides made since August 2005 in the United States. However, success in emergency management is highly dependent on the continuation of time, funding, and the attention of the general public and media, as well as consistency in political leadership. It is possible to have competently designed emergency response facilities, plans, and procedures, engaged and trained professional personnel, appropriately mitigated hazards, and an adequate amount of resources and material to support a catastrophic response and recovery, yet still fail. There is always the possibility that human error and hubris over recent successes can envelop an agency and make it complacent. Furthermore, mitigation plans, emergency operations and response plans, evacuation plans, recovery plans, and continuity plans cannot possibly account for all possible contingencies. Thus, the effective emergency manager in 2020 will attempt to forge strategic capability and develop the capacity of his or her organization to respond to forces that are beyond the organization’s and the community’s control.
